lede: Tasks people use AI for make up 23% of US wages. Pay hasn't changed more than usual, but the mix of jobs has shifted more than at any time since 2013. And 42% of new degrees are in fields that lead to the jobs most exposed to AI.
meaning: Use: AI use already covers tasks worth 23% of US pay, but most of it comes from a few hundred tasks.
Jobs: AI hasn't shown up in pay. The mix of jobs has shifted more than usual, though chance can't yet be ruled out, and job ads moved away from tasks AI can do before ChatGPT came out.

Training: The share of degrees and enrollment in exposed fields has risen slightly, so students have not moved away from them. Young workers' place in exposed jobs, against older workers', is 16% lower than in 2022.

items.title: Share of US wages in tasks people use AI for
items.note: Up from 18% in September 2025. A task counts once people use Claude for it at all, so this shows how widely AI use has spread across paid work, but not how much of that work AI does.
items.more: The Anthropic Economic Index sorts conversations with Claude into the job tasks the Labor Department lists for each occupation (O*NET). We add up what US workers earn on the tasks that appear, using the BLS wage tables. The June 2026 file leaves out rarely used tasks, so this figure uses March 2026, the most recent file that lists them all. Tasks people hand to Claude to do entirely account for 6% of US wages.
items.tech: Each occupation's OEWS wage bill is split across its O*NET tasks by frequency-weighted task shares, so task values sum exactly to the occupation's bill. Reach is the share of the national wage bill in tasks with any published usage; delegated reach scales each task by the share of its usage classed as automation. Claude.ai users are a selected population, so this describes where one platform's use falls.
items.src: Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026; OEWS wages, May 2025

items.title: Where AI use is heaviest
items.note: Complex problem solving skills account for 0.9% of AI use but only 0.3% of US wages, 2.5 times as much use as their share of pay. Physical abilities get the least, 0.3 times.
items.more: We sort job tasks into 25 skill groups and compare each group's share of AI use with its share of US wages. A value above 1 means people use AI on that group's tasks more than its share of pay alone would lead you to expect.
items.tech: Each task's labor is split across O*NET's 161 descriptors by the paper's gamma matrix, whose rows sum to one, and the descriptors roll up to 25 bundles, so neither usage nor wage dollars are lost in the mapping. The ratio is a bundle's share of usage over its share of the wage bill.

items.note: Three quarters of all AI use comes from just 243 tasks. Those tasks account for 3.1% of US wages, up from 1.8% in September 2025.

city.index_line: Whether pay, the mix of jobs and what job ads ask for have changed more than usual
city.why: If AI were already reshaping work, it would show up here first: in what employers pay for different skills, in which kinds of jobs grow, and in the tasks job ads ask for.
city.capline: Pay: no unusual change. Job mix: largest shift since 2013. Job ads: fell before ChatGPT.
city.mark: Pay: no unusual change. Job mix: largest shift since 2013.
city.headline: Pay hasn't changed more than usual, the mix of jobs has shifted more than at any time since 2013, and job ads turned away from tasks AI can do before ChatGPT came out.

items.title: Pay for different skills
items.note: If AI were changing what employers pay for, pay for some skills would be moving faster than usual. Between 2022 and 2025, none was. The biggest move, a drop in pay for analyzing information and making decisions, was smaller than the biggest move in seven of the ten earlier three-year periods since 2013. The reading for 2021 to 2024 was above the dashed line, so pay did move unusually then, but that has not carried into the latest period.
items.more: Every occupation uses a mix of 25 skill groups, from working with people to complex problem solving, as described in O*NET. From the wages BLS publishes for each occupation, we estimate what employers pay for each skill group. For each group, we compare the change over the last three years with its own changes since 2013, and call a change unusual only if it is bigger than 95% of the changes we get when we shuffle the years at random. These are averages over whole occupations, so a raise for new hires and a cut for people already in the job would cancel out.
items.tech: Relative pay is each bundle's log pay growth against the employment-weighted average, estimated for every annual transition from 2012 (13 transitions) on a balanced panel of occupations. The statistic is the largest, across the 25 bundles, of the mean of the last three transitions standardized by the bundle's own year-to-year variability. Its reference distribution relabels which three transitions are treated, using consecutive triples only, since pay changes are autocorrelated; the dashed line is that distribution's 95th percentile, and the chart divides the statistic by it, so 1.0 marks the line (p = 0.73 for the latest period).

items.title: Mix of jobs
items.note: Between 2022 and 2025, employment moved toward jobs that rely heavily on arts and humanities knowledge. It is the largest shift of all eleven three-year periods since 2013, which is as unusual as eleven periods can show. The reading for 2017 to 2020, which includes the first year of the pandemic, was also above the dashed line, so the spring 2027 wage tables will show whether this one lasts.
items.more: We measure how much of all US employment goes to each of the same 25 skill groups. That share changes when people move between occupations, which can happen before pay changes at all. It is tested the same way as pay, against each group's own history.
items.tech: The same statistic on employment-weighted bundle intensity. With 13 transitions there are 11 consecutive triples, so the smallest attainable p is 1/11; the latest period attains it (p = 0.09). The test cannot yet separate an AI effect from the post-pandemic reallocation of employment.

items.title: Job ads for tasks AI can do
items.note: From 2020 to the third quarter of 2022, job ads in the same occupation asked less and less often for tasks AI can do. ChatGPT's release in November 2022 brought no further drop, and by the third quarter of 2025 ads had recovered 68% of the decline.
items.more: The National Labor Exchange (NLx) data count how often ads in each occupation name each O*NET task. We check whether tasks AI can do lost ground to other tasks in the same occupation, and whether anything changed at ChatGPT's release. In 25 of the 55 earlier months, the same comparison showed a change at least as large as the one at the release.
items.tech: The paper's Appendix B: the gradient of a task's share of its occupation's ads on the task's Eloundou exposure, by quarter against 2019, so the comparison is within occupation by construction. The step at the release is measured against the sixteen months before it and set against the same step placed at each of 55 earlier months (p = 0.45). Occupation-months list at most fifty tasks, and the result holds on occupations whose lists are always complete.

city.how: For each of 25 skill groups, we compare the change in pay, and in the share of employment, over the last three years with that group's own history since 2013. A change counts as unusual only if it is bigger than nearly every earlier three-year period, which with the data since 2013 means the largest or close to it. Both are recalculated each spring, when BLS publishes new wage tables. For job ads, we measure how often ads in each occupation name each task, and check whether tasks AI can do lost ground at ChatGPT's release more than at earlier months.

items.title: New degrees in exposed fields
items.note: 41.8% of 2025 bachelor's degrees went to the third of fields whose graduates hold the most AI-exposed jobs, up from 40.7% in 2024.
items.more: Degrees by field come from the Education Department's IPEDS completions files. We score each field by the AI exposure of the jobs its graduates actually hold, using the Census Bureau's American Community Survey and the exposure measure of Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock (2023).
items.tech: Fields are six-digit CIP codes scored by the employment-weighted Eloundou exposure of the occupations ACS 2024 degree holders in each field actually work in, which measures where graduates go instead of where programs say they lead. Exposed fields are the top third of fields by that score.

items.title: Young workers in exposed jobs
items.note: Since 2022, workers aged 22 to 27 have lost ground in the jobs most exposed to AI, by 16% compared with workers aged 35 to 54.
items.more: From the Census Bureau's monthly Current Population Survey. For each age group we divide employment in the most exposed third of jobs by employment in all other jobs, then compare the young group's ratio with the older group's. Over the last 12 months the gap was 8.4 points wider than in the months before. In 1,000 random reorderings of the months, none produced a gap that large. The data start in January 2022, so they can't show whether the decline began before ChatGPT.
items.tech: The gauge is (E_young,exposed / E_young,other) / (E_prime,exposed / E_prime,other), with composited CPS weights, exposed meaning the top third of occupations on the Eloundou measure, Census codes mapped to SOC with OEWS employment weights, and the series indexed to 2022. The permutation relabels which months count as the last twelve at the level of CPS rotation groups, so the overlap between adjacent months' samples is kept under the null.
